title: The Record Is the Project's Memory, and Its Evidence
summary: Every claim, draw, audit, sale and defence a developer will ever make rests on records made at the time. Vera explains document control, the contemporaneous record and the transmittal, and shows how a small developer can run a record system that would satisfy a lender, a tribunal and a buyer's due diligence team.
body:
Mr Shabazz, memory fades, people leave and emails scatter. The record made at the time, filed where anyone can find it, is the only version of the project that survives. Build the system before the first drawing is issued.

Recall

Q. What is a dispute ladder?

A. A contractual sequence of steps, from negotiation through escalation, an independent expert or board and mediation, to arbitration or court, each with fixed time limits, so disagreements are filtered before they reach the costly rungs.

Q. Who should own a risk on the register?

A. One named person with the authority and resources to act on it, not a committee or a company, so that someone is accountable for watching its triggers and running its response.

Q. What is a deal pipeline?

A. A tracked list of potential deals at each stage, from first lead to closing, with dates and next actions, so a developer can see whether enough opportunities are moving to meet his goals.

Why this matters

Last week LEX showed that disputes are decided by evidence long before a hearing. That evidence is records. But records matter far beyond disputes. A lender releases a draw on records of work in place. An auditor signs on records of cost. A buyer pays the full price only if the due diligence data room proves the building is what you say it is. A tax authority accepts your treatment only if the documents support it. A developer with a poor record does not merely lose arguments; he pays more for money, sells for less and spends years answering questions he cannot prove.

Document control

Plain English: document control is the system that makes sure everyone works from the current version of every drawing, specification and contract document, and that you can prove what was issued to whom and when.

The professional framing has four parts.

  • A register. A single list of every controlled document with its number, title, current revision, status, such as for information or for construction, and date.
  • Revision control. Every change gets a new revision letter or number, with a short description of what changed, and superseded versions are marked and withdrawn from use.
  • Transmittals. A transmittal is a dated cover record listing exactly which documents, at which revisions, were sent to which recipients, for what purpose. It is the proof that a person received a drawing.
  • One home. A single shared location, with controlled access, that is the source of truth. Copies on laptops and in email are convenience, never the record.

A worked example, hypothetical. The structural engineer revises a beam schedule from revision C to revision D, increasing reinforcement at a transfer level. Without control, the revision goes by email to the contractor's project manager, who is on leave; the steel fixer works from revision C on a printed set. With control, revision D is uploaded to the shared register, revision C is stamped superseded, and a transmittal is issued to the contractor, the steel subcontractor and the owner's inspector, each of whom acknowledges. The inspector's hold-point checklist references the current revision. The error is caught before concrete arrives, and if it were not, the record shows exactly who received what and when.

Say that out loud now.

If I cannot prove who received which revision, and when, I do not have document control. I have a folder.

The contemporaneous record

A contemporaneous record is one made at or near the time of the event it describes, by someone with knowledge of it, in the normal course of work. Tribunals and courts give such records far more weight than witness memory or documents prepared later for the dispute. A daily site diary written that evening, a dated photograph with location, minutes circulated within two days of a meeting, a delivery ticket signed at the gate: these are contemporaneous. A summary written a year later, however accurate, is a reconstruction.

What a developer should require, at minimum: daily site reports from the contractor, covering weather, labour by trade, plant on site, work done, deliveries, visitors, instructions received and problems; weekly progress photographs from fixed points; minutes of every progress and design meeting, issued within two working days and corrected at the next meeting; a register of every instruction, request for information and change; and an owner's own log of decisions. Specify these in the contract, because a contractor will keep its own records for its own claims, and you want both sets to exist.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A contractor claims 40 days of delay for late answers to requests for information. The owner's register shows each request, the date received and the date answered: 31 of 34 answered within the contract's 7 days, 3 late by a total of 9 days, none on the critical path according to the contractor's own monthly schedules. The claim collapses not because the owner argued well, but because the record had already answered it.

How the best do it

Large owners and contractors on major projects commonly run a common data environment: a single controlled online space where every party publishes information, with defined states such as work in progress, shared, published and archived, and an audit trail of every action. International standards for information management in building projects, the ISO 19650 series, describe this approach. A small developer does not need the software of a megaproject to copy the discipline: one shared drive with a fixed folder structure, a document register in a spreadsheet, a naming convention, transmittals for every issue, and a rule that nothing counts as issued until it is in the register.

Omar's Six-Lens Check

Tax. Tax positions, especially capitalised costs and cross-border payments, stand or fall on contemporaneous documents; verify retention requirements against the primary source before you rely on them. Liability. Records are the defence against claims, from contractors, buyers and injured people. Banking. Lenders release money on records, and a weak record slows every draw. Governance. Minutes and resolutions prove that decisions were properly made by people with authority. Estate. Whoever inherits your interests must be able to find and understand the record. Exit. A complete data room supports price; a gap becomes a discount, an indemnity or an escrow.

What it costs to run

Hypothetically, on a 20,000,000 dollar project, a part-time document controller, perhaps one day a week rising to three in construction, plus a shared drive and a spreadsheet register, costs a small fraction of one percent of the budget. The first time it settles a disputed revision or answers a delay claim from the register, it has repaid itself many times over. The cost of no system is invisible until the day it is not: a rework order on a pour, a claim you cannot rebut, a buyer's lawyer asking for a document nobody can find. Budget the role as a line in soft costs at the start, and give the person authority to refuse to treat anything as issued until it is registered.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is records that exist but cannot be found or trusted: scattered across personal inboxes, phones and laptops, with no register and no proof of issue. The control is a single document home, a register with revision control, transmittals for every issue, contractually required daily reports and minutes, and a monthly check that the register matches what is on site.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that because everything is in email, everything is recorded. Email is a stream, not a record. It holds drafts, side conversations and attachments of unknown revision, and when a person leaves, their inbox often leaves with them.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the owner's decision log as part of the project charter. That log is the owner's own contemporaneous record. Together with the document register, it lets you answer the two questions every dispute asks: what did we know, and what did we decide, and when?

Recap

Records are the evidence for every claim, draw, audit, sale and defence. Document control means a register, revision control, transmittals and one home. Contemporaneous records, made at the time in the normal course of work, carry the most weight. Require them in the contract and check them monthly.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Grenfell Tower, and what happens when product records say one thing and the product does another.
checklist: One shared, access-controlled location is the single home of the project record.
Every controlled document is on a register with number, revision, status and date.
Superseded revisions are marked and withdrawn from use on site.
Every issue of documents goes with a dated transmittal and an acknowledgement.
The contract requires daily site reports, fixed-point photographs and prompt minutes.
I keep my own register of instructions, requests for information, changes and decisions.
Once a month I check that the register matches what is being built.
Nothing counts as issued until it is in the register.
head: Field checklist
speak: The record made at the time is the only version of the project that survives. Lenders release draws on it, auditors sign on it, buyers pay full price on it, and tribunals decide disputes on it. Document control has four parts: a register of every controlled document with its current revision; revision control, so superseded versions are marked and withdrawn; transmittals, the dated proof of exactly what was sent to whom; and one home, a single shared location that is the source of truth. Email is a stream, not a record. Then require contemporaneous records: daily site reports, fixed-point photographs, minutes issued within two days, and a register of instructions, requests for information and changes, plus your own decision log. A record made at the time, in the normal course of work, carries far more weight than anyone's memory. Build it before the first drawing is issued.
terms: Document control — the system ensuring everyone works from the current revision of every project document and that every issue can be proved.
Contemporaneous record — a record made at or near the time of an event, in the normal course of work, by someone with knowledge of it.
Transmittal — a dated cover record listing exactly which documents, at which revisions, were sent to which recipients and why.

hostile.q: Your contractor says it built to revision C because that is what it was given. Prove otherwise.
hostile.a: Our register shows revision D issued on the date stated, with a transmittal to the contractor's project manager and the steel subcontractor, both acknowledged the next day. Revision C was stamped superseded the same day, and the inspector's hold-point record for that pour cites revision D. I will send you the register extract, both transmittals, the acknowledgements and the hold-point sheet today.

title: Grenfell Tower 2017: When the Paperwork Described a Different Building
summary: On 14 June 2017 a fire at Grenfell Tower in London spread up the exterior cladding installed in a recent refurbishment, and 72 people died. The public inquiry's final report in 2024 found that misleading product test evidence and certificates, and a chain of parties who relied on them without checking, were central to the disaster. Ford and Cole take it through seven steps as a failure of records.
body:
At Grenfell, documents said products were suitable, and many people relied on documents that did not describe what was being built. A record is only evidence if someone checks that it matches reality.

Recall

Q. What is a transmittal?

A. A dated cover record listing exactly which documents, at which revisions, were sent to which recipients and why. It is the proof that someone received a particular version.

Q. What does a standstill agreement do?

A. It pauses a limitation period for a defined time by agreement, so that settlement talks can continue without either side losing the right to bring a claim.

Q. What does a contingency plan for contractor default include?

A. Security to call, such as a bond or letter of credit, a list of replacement contractors, current records of work in place and materials on site, and step-in rights over subcontracts.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me today, and we approach this case with care. Seventy-two people died. We use it because its final report is the clearest public account of what happens when the record of a building, its test reports, certificates, product literature and approvals, drifts away from the building itself, and when every party assumes someone else has checked. This lesson draws on the public inquiry's reports; read them yourself, because a summary cannot carry their detail. The building was in England, under English regulation, which is not the code basis this course uses, but the failure of records is universal.

1. Timeline

Grenfell Tower was a residential tower block in North Kensington, completed in the 1970s. A refurbishment completed in 2016 added new windows and an external cladding system: aluminium composite panels with a polyethylene core over combustible insulation, with a ventilated cavity between. On the night of 14 June 2017, a fire began in a kitchen appliance in a flat on the fourth floor. It escaped through the window area into the cladding and spread up and around the building within minutes. Seventy-two people died. A public inquiry was established. Its first-phase report, in October 2019, examined the night itself. Its second-phase report, published in September 2024, examined how the building came to be in that condition.

2. Key decisions

The decisions that mattered were the selection of the cladding and insulation products, the acceptance of each product's suitability for a building of that height, and the regulatory approval of the refurbishment. The inquiry's final report examined each, and found that at no stage did anyone with responsibility rigorously test the evidence of suitability against the actual system being installed.

3. Assumptions

Each party assumed the documents were right and that someone else had verified them. Designers and contractors relied on manufacturers' literature and certificates. Building control relied on the professionals. Certification bodies relied on test evidence supplied by manufacturers. The inquiry found that this chain of reliance was hollow: in its words and findings, some manufacturers had engaged in systematic dishonesty about the fire performance of their products, including presenting test results from configurations that did not match the products as marketed, and withholding unfavourable test results; verify the detail against the report itself.

4. Incentives

Manufacturers had a commercial incentive to secure a market for their products on tall buildings. Certification and testing bodies were paid by the companies whose products they assessed. The refurbishment was under cost pressure, which the inquiry examined. Designers and contractors had an incentive to rely on certificates rather than commission expensive independent analysis. Regulators had an incentive to keep guidance stable. Each incentive pushed toward trusting the paper.

Cole's point: when the party producing the evidence is paid by the party whose interest it serves, the evidence is a claim, not a fact.

Say that out loud now.

A certificate is a claim about a product. It becomes evidence only when I check what was tested against what is being built.

5. Warning signs ignored

The inquiry's reports describe warnings across years: earlier fires involving combustible cladding on tall buildings in several countries, unfavourable test results known to some in industry, and concerns raised about the clarity of the official guidance on what materials were acceptable on high-rise external walls. None of these led the parties involved in the refurbishment to demand primary test evidence for the exact system proposed.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return, for the building, was the installation of the cladding system without verified evidence that the system as built would resist fire spread. After that, the building's safety depended on a fire never reaching the facade. For the record, the point of no return was earlier: the first time a party accepted a certificate or brochure as proof without reading what had actually been tested.

7. Root cause

The inquiry's findings point to a system failure across government, industry and the professions, not a single error. Seen through this week's lens, the root cause was that the project's records of product performance were not evidence of the building's performance, and no one in the chain was required, or chose, to close that gap. The paper described a different building.

Cole's view: reading a test report

The practical discipline for a developer is simple to state and tedious to do. For every safety-critical product, especially in the envelope and fire strategy, ask for the primary test report, not the brochure or the certificate summary. Read four things: what exactly was tested, including every layer and fixing; what standard and configuration; what the result was and any limitations stated; and who paid for and conducted the test. Then compare that, line by line, with the specified and installed system. Where they differ, the evidence does not apply, and an engineer must say what does. On American projects, that review sits with the fire protection engineer and the architect against the adopted code and referenced standards; verify against the current adopted edition. Professional sign-off required: fire protection engineer and envelope consultant.

What changed afterwards, and why it is about records

An independent review of building regulations and fire safety, commissioned after the fire and published in 2018, called for a golden thread of information: an accurate, up-to-date digital record of a higher-risk building, kept from design through its whole life, so that anyone responsible for it can see what was actually built and why. England later legislated a new regime for higher-risk buildings built around that idea; verify the current requirements against the primary source before you rely on them. The point for you is not English law. It is that, after one of the deadliest residential fires in modern British history, the fix that regulators reached for was a better record.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a chain of reliance in which every party trusts a document that nobody has compared with the actual system. The control is a product evidence register for safety-critical items: primary test report, configuration tested, configuration installed, differences, and the named engineer who accepted any difference, kept in the project record.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats a certificate, a stamp or a brochure as the end of the question. It is the start. The second beginner's mistake is allowing a substitute product during value engineering without re-running the evidence for the new product in the new configuration.

Callback

In Week 6 and again in Week 49, the Hyatt Regency walkways showed how a change nobody re-checked can kill. Grenfell is the same lesson applied to the record: a substitution, a certificate and a chain of assumptions, each reasonable alone, with no one responsible for confirming that the evidence still matched the thing being built.

Recap

At Grenfell, combustible cladding and insulation installed in a refurbishment carried fire up the building in 2017, and 72 people died. The 2024 final report found misleading product evidence and a chain of reliance that never tested it. For a developer, a record is evidence only when it is checked against reality.

Rule 82: Never accept a test report, certificate or product claim as evidence until you have read what was actually tested, in what configuration, and confirmed it matches what is being installed; then keep that comparison in the project record.

Next: Nadia on The Money: what records cost, what they save, and how they show up in price.
checklist: I keep a product evidence register for every safety-critical item.
I ask for the primary test report, not only a certificate or brochure.
I check what was tested, to what standard, in what configuration and with what limitations.
I compare the tested configuration with the specified and installed system, line by line.
A named engineer must accept, in writing, any difference between tested and installed.
Any product substitution re-opens the evidence for the new configuration.
I note who paid for each test and treat the result as a claim until verified.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 14 June 2017 a fire at Grenfell Tower in London spread up cladding installed in a recent refurbishment, and 72 people died. The public inquiry's final report in 2024 found that some manufacturers had been dishonest about fire performance, including presenting tests that did not match the products as marketed, and that designers, contractors, certifiers and regulators relied on documents nobody tested against the actual system. Every incentive pushed toward trusting the paper. For a developer, the lesson is that a certificate is a claim about a product, not proof about your building. For every safety-critical item, read the primary test report: what was tested, in what configuration, with what result and limits, and who paid. Compare it line by line with what is installed. Rule 82: never accept a test report, certificate or product claim until you have checked it matches what is being installed, and keep that comparison in the record.
terms: Primary test report — the full report of a test as conducted, including the exact configuration, standard, results and limitations, as opposed to a summary or certificate.
Chain of reliance — a sequence of parties each relying on another's document or approval, so that an error in the first document passes unchecked through all of them.
Product evidence register — a record listing, for each safety-critical product, the test evidence, the configuration tested and installed, and who accepted any difference.

hostile.q: Your envelope consultant approved this cladding system on the strength of the manufacturer's certificate. Why should my insurer accept that as evidence?
hostile.a: It should not, and neither do I. Our product evidence register has the primary test report for each layer, the configuration tested and the configuration installed, side by side. Where they differed at one parapet detail, our fire protection engineer issued a written assessment, which is in the register with his name and date. I will send you the register and the three underlying reports today, and our engineer will take your questions directly.

rule: Rule 82: Never accept a test report, certificate or product claim as evidence until you have read what was actually tested, in what configuration, and confirmed it matches what is being installed; then keep that comparison in the project record.

title: What Records Are Worth in Dollars
summary: Records look like overhead until you price what their absence costs. Nadia shows how a gap in the record becomes a slower draw, a lost claim, a qualified audit and a discount at sale, and works two examples through interest cost and cap-rate value. Warrick's Wealth Ledger turns the same discipline on your personal tax basis.
body:
Every missing record eventually becomes a number: interest paid while a draw waits, a claim you cannot prove, or net operating income a buyer refuses to pay for. Price the gap before you decide the record is too expensive to keep.

Recall

Q. What is a contemporaneous record?

A. A record made at or near the time of an event, in the normal course of work, by someone with knowledge of it. It carries far more weight than later recollection.

Q. How do you value a claim?

A. Probability of success times the realistic award, plus expected cost recovery, discounted for time, adjusted for the risk of not collecting, less fees.

Q. Why does a developer keep a relationship log for brokers and institutions?

A. So that commitments made, information shared and deals shown are on record, which protects fee arrangements and makes follow-up reliable when people change roles.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, finance people and project people see records differently. The project manager sees filing. I see a balance sheet. Every number in your accounts, every capitalised cost, every capital account, every lease in a rent roll, is only as good as the document behind it. When the document is missing, the number is an assertion, and lenders, auditors, buyers and tax authorities price assertions at a discount.

Where records show up in the numbers

Plain English: a record pays you in four ways. It gets you paid faster, it lets you recover money owed, it lowers the cost of being checked, and it supports the price when you sell.

  • Draw speed. A lender funds a draw only when the package is complete: payment application, lien waivers, invoices, the monitor's report. A missing document delays the draw, and the contractor or your equity carries the gap.
  • Claim recovery. As Week 81 showed, a claim is worth its probability of success, and probability is mostly evidence.
  • Audit and review cost. Auditors charge for time. A clean record shortens the audit; a messy one lengthens it and can lead to a qualified opinion, which is a formal statement that the auditor could not verify part of the accounts.
  • Exit value. A buyer pays for net operating income (NOI) it can verify. Unverified income is excluded, discounted or held back in escrow.

Worked example 1: the slow draw

Hypothetical. A 20,000,000 dollar construction loan at 7 percent a year. Each month the developer submits a draw of about 1,000,000 dollars, and each month it is delayed 10 days because lien waivers from subcontractors arrive late. The contractor, short of cash, asks the developer to bridge the gap, which he does from a revolving credit line at 10 percent.

  1. Bridged amount: 1,000,000 dollars.
  2. Cost of bridging for 10 days at 10 percent a year: 1,000,000 times 0.10 times 10 divided by 365, about 2,700 dollars.
  3. Over 18 months of draws: about 49,000 dollars.
  4. Add the contractor's own reaction: a contractor paid late prices its next job higher or slows its crews, which no ledger shows.

About 49,000 dollars is modest against a 20,000,000 dollar loan. It is not modest against the cost of the fix: a lien-waiver checklist on the contractor's payment application form and a rule that subcontractors are paid only against signed waivers. The fix costs almost nothing.

Say that out loud now.

A missing record is never free. It is a number I have not priced yet.

Worked example 2: the discount at sale

Hypothetical. You sell a stabilised apartment building with 1,500,000 dollars of NOI at an agreed capitalisation rate, the ratio of NOI to value, of 6 percent, implying a price of 25,000,000 dollars. In due diligence the buyer's team finds that 12 of the 100 leases have no signed copy on file, only entries in the rent roll, and that three units carry rent concessions not shown in the rent roll.

The buyer reasons as follows. The 12 unsigned leases carry 180,000 dollars of annual rent. Until signed leases are produced, the buyer excludes that income or, at best, demands an escrow. Excluding it lowers verified NOI to 1,320,000 dollars. At 6 percent, value falls to 22,000,000 dollars: a 3,000,000 dollar price reduction from 180,000 dollars of undocumented income. The concessions, undisclosed, also raise the question of what else is missing, and the buyer adds a broader indemnity and a longer escrow.

Even if you can obtain signatures from the tenants within weeks, you have lost leverage, delayed closing and paid for the buyer's extra legal work. The data room is the record of your asset, and its gaps are priced at the cap rate.

The cost of keeping records well

Hypothetically, a part-time document controller and a property manager's lease file audit together cost perhaps 30,000 to 60,000 dollars a year on a project of this size; these are illustrative figures, not benchmarks. Set that against one month of interest on a delayed draw, one lost claim or one percent of a sale price, and the return on the record is very high. The difficulty is that the cost is certain and visible, and the saving is uncertain and invisible, so it is the first budget line cut under pressure. Protect it with a named role and a budget line from day one.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

The same discipline applies to your personal balance sheet. When you eventually sell an investment, the tax on the gain usually depends on its cost base: what you paid plus allowable additions, such as certain capital improvements. Without the records of those additions, you may be unable to claim them, and you pay tax on a gain partly made of your own money; how cost base is defined and what qualifies varies by jurisdiction, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Keep, for every personal investment and every capital contribution to a project company, the purchase documents, contribution receipts, distribution statements and any capital improvement invoices, in one place, for as long as an adviser tells you to. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

A third, shorter example: the audit

Hypothetical. An auditor budgets 120 hours to audit a project company with clean records: a fixed asset register reconciled to invoices, capitalised costs supported by approved change orders, and bank reconciliations done monthly. The same company with scattered records needs 200 hours, because each sample item must be chased. At an illustrative 250 dollars an hour, the gap is 20,000 dollars a year. Worse, if the auditor cannot verify a capitalised cost line, it may qualify the opinion, and a qualified opinion can breach a reporting covenant in the loan agreement or an investor agreement. A few thousand dollars of monthly reconciliation buys a clean opinion, and a clean opinion protects your cost of capital for the next deal.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating record-keeping as overhead to be cut, so the cost of the gap appears years later, at sale, audit or claim, when it is many times larger and cannot be fixed. The control is a named budget line and a named person for records from day one, and a pre-sale data-room audit a year before any planned exit.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes the rent roll is the record. The rent roll is a summary. The record is the signed lease, every amendment and every concession letter, and a buyer will ask for all of them.

Callback

In Week 10, Sage taught that value equals NOI divided by the cap rate. Today's second example is that formula run backwards: 180,000 dollars of undocumented income, divided by a 6 percent cap rate, became a 3,000,000 dollar price question. Every dollar of NOI you cannot prove is worth roughly sixteen times that dollar in price.

Recap

Records pay through faster draws, recoverable claims, cheaper audits and supported prices. A 10-day draw delay cost about 49,000 dollars of bridging; 180,000 dollars of undocumented rent cost 3,000,000 dollars of value at a 6 percent cap rate. Budget the record from day one, and keep your personal cost-base records with the same care.

Next: Vera on The Rules: privilege, the duty to preserve, spoliation and retention.
checklist: I price every record gap as interest, lost recovery, audit cost or lost value.
Lien waivers are required with every payment application before a draw is submitted.
Every lease, amendment and concession letter is filed signed, not only in the rent roll.
I run a data-room audit a year before any planned sale.
Record-keeping has a named person and a budget line from day one.
I keep cost-base records for every personal investment and capital contribution.
I protect the records budget when costs are cut.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every missing record eventually becomes a number. Records pay four ways: faster draws, claims you can prove, cheaper audits, and a price a buyer will pay. Example one: a draw delayed 10 days a month because lien waivers arrive late, bridged at 10 percent, costs about 49,000 dollars over 18 months, and the fix is a waiver checklist that costs almost nothing. Example two: a building with 1,500,000 dollars of NOI at a 6 percent cap rate, priced at 25,000,000 dollars. The buyer finds 12 unsigned leases carrying 180,000 dollars of rent and excludes it. Verified NOI falls to 1,320,000, and value to 22,000,000. That is 3,000,000 dollars from paperwork. The cost of records is certain and visible; the saving is uncertain and invisible, so it gets cut first. Protect it with a named person and a budget line, and keep your personal cost-base records the same way.
terms: Qualified opinion — an auditor's formal statement that part of the financial statements could not be verified or does not comply, which lowers their credibility.
Data room — the organised collection of documents a seller provides to a buyer's due diligence team, physically or online.
Cost base — the amount treated as the cost of an investment for tax purposes, usually what was paid plus allowable additions.

hostile.q: Twelve of your leases have no signed copy. Why should I pay for income I cannot verify?
hostile.a: You should not pay for it until it is verified, and I am not asking you to. I propose we hold back the value of those 12 leases in escrow, sized at your cap rate, and release it lease by lease as signed copies are delivered within 60 days. I have already sent estoppel requests to those tenants confirming rent and terms. The other 88 leases and every concession letter are in the data room, indexed to the rent roll.

title: Privilege, Preservation and Retention
summary: Three rules decide what happens to your records in a dispute: which ones you can keep confidential, which ones you must keep, and for how long. Vera explains legal privilege and how it is lost, the duty to preserve once a dispute is reasonably anticipated, the consequences of destroying evidence, and how to set a retention schedule without guessing at legal periods.
body:
In a dispute, most of your project record will be seen by the other side. A narrow category is protected by privilege, all relevant records must be preserved once trouble is foreseeable, and destroying them is worse than anything they could have shown.

Recall

Q. What does a buyer do with income it cannot verify in due diligence?

A. It excludes it from the NOI it pays for, discounts it, or holds part of the price back in escrow until the documents are produced, and the effect on price is the excluded income divided by the cap rate.

Q. What was Rule 81?

A. The day a claim becomes possible, diarise its notice period and limitation period, and never let talks run past either without a signed standstill agreement or a filed claim.

Q. What is the risk of relying on a single broker?

A. The broker controls what you see and when, and its incentive is to close, so you may miss better deals or pay a price set by the broker's timetable.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer who understands these three rules sends the right emails, keeps the right files and avoids the one mistake that can lose a case on its own: losing or destroying documents after a dispute was foreseeable. These rules differ by jurisdiction and by forum, courts and arbitration treat them differently, and the details matter. Everything here is conceptual. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, and take advice from dispute counsel before any document decision in a live or threatened dispute.

Privilege: what you can keep confidential

Plain English: privilege is a legal right to refuse to disclose certain communications, even to a court or tribunal. In common law systems it usually takes two main forms, though names and boundaries vary.

  • Legal advice privilege. Confidential communications between a client and its lawyer, made for the purpose of giving or receiving legal advice.
  • Litigation privilege. Confidential communications, which can include those with third parties such as experts, made for the dominant purpose of existing or reasonably anticipated litigation; whether and how it applies to arbitration varies.

The professional framing is about what privilege does not cover. Business documents are not privileged because a lawyer was copied. A project manager's email to the contractor is not privileged because it was later sent to counsel. A consultant's report prepared for project purposes is generally not privileged, even if it later becomes central to a dispute. And privilege can be lost, or waived, by sharing the advice outside the protected circle, for example by forwarding counsel's opinion to the contractor to strengthen your negotiating position.

A worked example, hypothetical. After defects appear, the developer emails his lawyer: "Please advise on our rights against the contractor; attached is the consultant's report." The email seeking advice is likely privileged; the attached consultant's report, prepared earlier for project purposes, likely is not, and must be produced if relevant. The lawyer's reply is likely privileged. Then the developer forwards the reply to his investors with a comment, and to the contractor's director to show him the strength of the claim. The first forward may or may not preserve privilege depending on the relationship and any common-interest arrangement; the second almost certainly waives it. Mark advice as privileged, keep it in a separate folder, and share it only on counsel's instruction.

Say that out loud now.

Copying a lawyer does not make a document privileged. Sharing advice outside the circle can lose the privilege.

Preservation: what you must keep

In many systems, once a dispute or litigation is reasonably anticipated, a party must preserve documents that may be relevant to it, including electronic ones. The usual tool is a litigation hold: a written instruction to everyone who holds relevant material to stop deleting, overwriting or discarding it, and to suspend routine deletion, until counsel releases the hold.

The difficulty is scope and medium. Relevant material includes email, but also text and messaging apps on personal phones, photographs, drawings in every revision, schedule files in their native format, accounting entries and the metadata that shows when files were created or changed. A hold that covers the office server and ignores the site manager's phone is a hold with a hole in it.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A contractor's delay claim arrives. The developer's practice is to auto-delete messages on the project messaging group after 90 days, and his site manager changes phones every year. Within days, counsel issues a hold: auto-delete is suspended, the site manager's phone is imaged before it is replaced, and the shared drive's version history is exported. Six months later, the contractor alleges it gave an instruction by message that the developer denies receiving. The preserved messages show the instruction was sent to a different group. Without the hold, the absence of the message would have looked like destruction.

Spoliation: what happens if you do not

Spoliation is the destruction, alteration or loss of relevant evidence once there is a duty to preserve it. Consequences vary by system and forum, but can include the tribunal drawing an adverse inference, which means assuming the missing document would have hurt the party that lost it, costs orders, exclusion of evidence and, in serious deliberate cases, more severe sanctions. A tribunal that concludes a party destroyed evidence will often doubt everything else that party says. Treat preservation as a rule you never break, not a cost to weigh.

Retention: how long to keep

A retention schedule is a written list of record categories, how long each is kept and how it is destroyed when the period ends. Legal minimums come from several directions: tax, corporate law, employment, health and safety, and the limitation periods for construction claims, which for latent defects can run long after completion. Lenders, investor agreements and insurers may add contractual periods. Do not guess any of these numbers [unverified — confirm independently]. Ask counsel and your accountant for each category, take the longest that applies, and add a margin.

Two principles hold regardless of jurisdiction. First, routine destruction under a schedule is legitimate, and evidence that you follow it is itself protective. Second, any destruction stops the moment a hold applies, whatever the schedule says. For a developer, the safe practice is to keep the core project record, contracts, drawings at final revision, as-built records, test and commissioning reports, warranties and correspondence on claims, for at least the longest construction limitation period that could apply, and often for the life of ownership.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is routine deletion continuing after a dispute became foreseeable, especially on phones and messaging apps, so a party with a good case looks like a party hiding evidence. The control is a written litigation-hold procedure, triggered by counsel the day a claim is threatened, that suspends auto-deletion, images personal devices used for project work and confirms receipt from every custodian.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner marks every email "privileged and confidential" and assumes that protects it. Labels do not create privilege; purpose and audience do. The second beginner's mistake is running a project on personal messaging accounts with no thought for how those messages would be preserved or produced.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught engagement letters and privilege as part of using professionals well. Today extends that lesson: the engagement letter defines the protected circle, and every forward of advice either stays inside it or breaks it.

Recap

Privilege protects confidential lawyer-client advice and some litigation communications, not business documents, and it can be waived by sharing. Once a dispute is reasonably anticipated, preserve everything relevant, including phones and messages, under a written hold. Spoliation can cost you the case. Set retention by category with advice, take the longest period, and never destroy under a hold. Professional sign-off required: dispute counsel in the relevant jurisdiction.

Next: Petra on The Numbers: reverse engineering a delay award to see which records would have changed it.
checklist: I keep legal advice in a separate folder, marked privileged, shared only on counsel's instruction.
I never forward counsel's advice to a counterparty to strengthen my position.
I know copying a lawyer does not make a business document privileged.
Counsel issues a written litigation hold the day a claim is threatened.
The hold covers phones, messaging apps, native schedule files and metadata.
Auto-deletion is suspended and personal devices used for work are preserved.
My retention schedule is set by category with advice, taking the longest period.
Nothing is destroyed under a hold, whatever the schedule says.
head: Field checklist
speak: In a dispute, most of your record will be seen by the other side, so know three rules. First, privilege. Confidential advice between you and your lawyer is usually protected, and so are some communications made for litigation. Business documents are not, even if a lawyer was copied, and forwarding counsel's advice to the contractor can waive the protection. Second, preservation. Once a dispute is reasonably foreseeable, you must keep everything relevant, and the tool is a written litigation hold that suspends auto-deletion and captures phones, messaging apps and native files. Third, spoliation. Destroying or losing evidence after that point can lead a tribunal to assume the worst and doubt everything else you say. Then retention: a written schedule by category, set with advice, taking the longest period that applies, and never applied while a hold is in force.
terms: Privilege — a legal right to refuse to disclose certain communications, chiefly confidential lawyer-client advice and some communications made for litigation.
Litigation hold — a written instruction to everyone holding relevant material to stop deleting or discarding it, and to suspend routine deletion, until released by counsel.
Spoliation — the destruction, alteration or loss of relevant evidence after a duty to preserve it has arisen.

hostile.q: Your site manager's messages for the six months before our claim are missing. Why should the tribunal not assume they show you received our instruction?
hostile.a: Because they are not missing. Counsel issued a litigation hold the week your claim was threatened, auto-deletion was suspended and the site manager's phone was imaged before it was replaced. The full export, with metadata, has been produced. It shows your instruction was sent to a different group, of which he was not a member. I am happy for your expert to examine the image.

title: Reverse Engineering a Delay Award
summary: A hypothetical tribunal awards a contractor 70 of its 90 claimed days and 760,000 dollars. Petra works backward from the award to find which days the owner lost, why each was lost, and which missing records would have changed the result, then prices what those records would have cost to keep.
body:
Work backward from an award and you find that most of an owner's loss was not argument. It was days the owner could not disprove, because nobody wrote them down at the time.

Recall

Q. What is a litigation hold?

A. A written instruction, usually from counsel, to everyone holding relevant material to stop deleting or discarding it and to suspend routine deletion, once a dispute is reasonably anticipated.

Q. In a delay claim, what is the difference between compensable and excusable delay?

A. Compensable delay gives the contractor both extra time and money; excusable delay gives time only, so no liquidated damages, but no extra payment. The contract and governing law decide which applies.

Q. What is the business development lesson of a lost deal?

A. That a deal lost on price, timing or trust usually has a cause you can trace, and recording why you lost it improves the next pursuit.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even-numbered week, so we reverse engineer: start from a finished outcome and work backward. The outcome is an arbitral award against an owner. Every figure is hypothetical. The point is to see, line by line, where the owner's record failed, so that you build a record on your own projects that would have won those lines.

The finished outcome

A contractor on a 22-month residential job finished 90 days late and claimed 90 days of compensable delay. The owner argued that 40 of those days were the contractor's own, caused by a shortage of crews and late steel deliveries. The tribunal awarded the contractor 70 compensable days at 9,000 dollars a day of prolongation, plus 130,000 dollars of disruption: 760,000 dollars. It allowed the owner liquidated damages for the remaining 20 days at 5,000 dollars a day: 100,000 dollars. Net to the contractor: 660,000 dollars, plus a share of its costs.

The owner had expected, on its own analysis, to concede about 50 days. The award gave 20 more compensable days. Our task: explain the 20 days and what they cost.

Step 1: price the gap

Each extra compensable day cost the owner twice: 9,000 dollars of prolongation paid to the contractor, and 5,000 dollars of liquidated damages the owner did not receive. That is 14,000 dollars a day. Twenty days times 14,000 dollars equals 280,000 dollars, before the owner's share of costs and its own fees on the lost issues. Call it 350,000 dollars all in.

Say that out loud now.

Each day I could not disprove cost me the contractor's daily rate plus the liquidated damages I did not collect.

Step 2: find which days were lost

The award's reasons show three blocks of disputed time.

  1. Crew shortage, claimed by the owner as 15 days of contractor delay on the frame. The tribunal accepted 5. It found the owner's evidence of crew numbers was anecdotal, from a witness, while the contractor produced its own daily labour returns showing adequate crews.
  2. Late steel deliveries, claimed by the owner as 15 days. The tribunal accepted none. The owner could not show the planned delivery dates or when steel actually arrived; the contractor's narrative attributed the delay to late shop drawing approval by the owner's engineer.
  3. Concurrency at the end of the job, 10 days, during which the owner argued both sides were delaying. The tribunal accepted 15 days of contractor delay here, more than the owner claimed, because the owner's own monthly schedules, which the contractor had updated, showed the contractor's facade work as critical.

Owner's claim: 40 contractor days. Accepted: 20. Lost: 20, mostly in blocks 1 and 2.

Step 3: why each block was lost

Block 1 was lost on the quality of evidence. The tribunal preferred the contractor's contemporaneous labour returns over the owner's witness memory. The owner had the right to require daily reports under the contract, received them, and never checked them against what its own inspector saw. Some of the contractor's returns showed full crews on days the owner's inspector, if he had recorded it, would have shown half.

Block 2 was lost on the absence of evidence. No delivery register existed. The owner's engineer's shop drawing log had approval dates, but not submission dates, so the owner could not show the drawings were submitted late by the contractor rather than approved late by the engineer. The contractor's version stood unopposed.

Block 3 shows the other side of the coin: where the record existed, it decided the point, even against the owner's expectations.

Step 4: the records that would have changed it

Work forward again from the reasons. Three records, kept at the time, would most likely have recovered most of the 20 days:

  • An owner's inspector's daily diary recording headcount by trade, checked weekly against the contractor's labour returns, with any discrepancy raised in writing.
  • A delivery register for long-lead items: planned date, actual date, delivery ticket reference, and a photograph at the gate.
  • A submittal log recording, for every shop drawing, the date submitted, date returned, revision and status, so that review time and resubmission time are separated.

Suppose, conservatively, that these records would have won 15 of the 20 lost days. At 14,000 dollars a day that is 210,000 dollars of award, plus some of the costs.

Step 5: price the records

Now price the remedy. An owner's inspector already on site for quality spends perhaps 30 minutes a day on a headcount diary. A delivery register and a submittal log are spreadsheets maintained by the document controller, perhaps two hours a week between them. Over 22 months, hypothetically, the incremental cost is a few hundred hours, perhaps 25,000 to 40,000 dollars at illustrative rates. Against a likely 210,000 dollars recovered, plus a stronger negotiating position long before arbitration, the return is several times the cost. And the records would also have helped the owner manage the job, because a crew shortage spotted in week two is a conversation, not a claim.

Checking the arithmetic aloud

Read the chain once more, slowly, because a tribunal will. Ninety days late. Seventy days compensable at 9,000 dollars is 630,000 dollars, plus 130,000 dollars of disruption, gives 760,000 dollars. Twenty days of contractor delay at 5,000 dollars of liquidated damages gives 100,000 dollars to the owner. Net, 660,000 dollars to the contractor. The owner's own forecast had been 50 compensable days: 450,000 dollars of prolongation, plus the same disruption, less 40 days of liquidated damages at 200,000 dollars, a net of 380,000 dollars. The difference between forecast and award is 280,000 dollars, which is exactly the 20 days at 14,000 dollars. When the reconciliation closes to the dollar, you have understood the award.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is collecting the contractor's records without keeping your own, so the only contemporaneous evidence of what happened on site is the other side's. The control is an owner's daily diary, a delivery register and a submittal log that separates submission from review, each checked weekly against the contractor's reports, with discrepancies raised in writing at the time.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner relies on a witness to remember what happened two years ago. Tribunals prefer documents made at the time, and a careful contractor will have them. The second beginner's mistake is treating the contractor's daily reports as a formality to file rather than evidence to check.

Callback

On Day 5 of Week 81, Quincy valued a delay claim component by component, starting with entitlement to time. This lesson shows where that time is won or lost: not in the analysis, but in the record the analysis is built from. A time impact analysis is only as good as the dates you can prove.

Recap

Working backward from a 660,000 dollar net award, 20 extra compensable days cost the owner about 14,000 dollars each. They were lost because the owner had a witness against the contractor's labour returns, no delivery register and a submittal log without submission dates. Three simple records, costing a fraction of the loss, would likely have recovered most of it. Professional sign-off required: forensic scheduler and dispute counsel.

Next: Vera in The Room: the meeting the day a claim arrives, and the litigation hold.
checklist: My inspector keeps a daily diary of headcount by trade.
I check the contractor's labour returns against my own diary every week.
I raise discrepancies in writing at the time, not at the hearing.
I keep a delivery register for long-lead items with tickets and gate photos.
My submittal log records submission and review dates separately.
I price a lost day as the contractor's daily rate plus my lost liquidated damages.
I review the record against likely claims every month, not after a dispute starts.
head: Field checklist
speak: Work backward from an award and you find most of an owner's loss was days it could not disprove. In the example, the contractor finished 90 days late. The owner argued 40 days were the contractor's own; the tribunal accepted 20. Each lost day cost the owner 9,000 dollars of prolongation plus 5,000 dollars of liquidated damages it never collected, so 20 days was about 280,000 dollars before costs. Why? On crew shortages, the owner had a witness and the contractor had daily labour returns. On late steel, there was no delivery register, and the submittal log had approval dates but no submission dates. Three records, kept at the time, would likely have won most of those days: an owner's daily headcount diary checked against the contractor's returns, a delivery register, and a submittal log that separates submission from review. They cost a fraction of what was lost.
terms: Daily labour return — the contractor's daily record of workers on site by trade, a key piece of contemporaneous evidence in delay disputes.
Submittal log — a register of shop drawings and other submissions with dates submitted, returned, revision and status.
Delivery register — a log of planned and actual delivery dates for key materials, with ticket references and photographs.

hostile.q: Your owner says our crews were short for weeks. Our labour returns say otherwise. What have you got besides your inspector's memory?
hostile.a: His daily diary, written each afternoon, recording headcount by trade, and the weekly emails in which we raised every discrepancy with your site manager at the time. On the fourteen days in dispute, the diary shows between nine and twelve on the frame against the eighteen your returns state, and your site manager acknowledged two of those emails. We will produce the diary in native form with its creation dates.

title: The Morning the Claim Arrives
summary: A contractor's formal claim lands at 8 in the morning. By 10 the developer has his project team in a room, and someone suggests tidying up the files. Vera scripts the meeting: what to say, what never to say, the question behind the team's questions, when to stay silent, and how to hold your state when you are angry.
body:
The first two hours after a claim arrives decide whether your record is evidence or a liability. Your job in the room is to stop anything being deleted, written or said that you will have to explain later.

Recall

Q. Why did the owner lose block 2 of the delay award in Day 5?

A. Because no delivery register existed and the submittal log had approval dates but not submission dates, so the owner could not show the delay was the contractor's.

Q. Does copying a lawyer on an email make it privileged?

A. No. Privilege depends on the purpose and confidentiality of the communication, not on who is copied. Business documents remain disclosable.

Q. What is a reference class in the outside view?

A. A set of similar past cases whose actual outcomes are used to forecast a new one, rather than relying on the inside view of the plan.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a claim arrives, people react. The project manager feels blamed. The site manager wants to defend his decisions. Someone remembers an email they now wish they had not sent. In that hour, well-meaning people do the three most damaging things in dispute practice: they delete, they rewrite, and they send angry messages. You lead the room. What you say in the first meeting sets what the team does for the next two years.

The scene

Hypothetical. At 8 in the morning, your contractor's formal notice of claim arrives: 2,400,000 dollars and 120 days, alleging late design and owner interference. At 10 you meet your project manager, site manager, document controller and owner's inspector. Counsel joins by phone at 10:30. The project manager opens: "Half of this is rubbish. But some of our emails from March look bad. Should we clean up the shared drive before their lawyers see it?"

The lines to say

  • "Nobody deletes, edits, moves or renames anything from this moment, on the drive, in email or on your phones. That includes messages you think are personal."
  • "Counsel will send a written hold today. Please reply to it confirming you have read it."
  • "If you sent something you now regret, tell counsel, not each other. A bad email that is preserved can be explained. A deleted one cannot."
  • "We do not reply to the contractor today. We acknowledge receipt and say we will respond in accordance with the contract."
  • "From now on, put facts in writing and opinions in conversation with counsel."

The lines never to say

  • "Let's tidy up the files." Whatever is meant, it will be described later as an instruction to destroy evidence.
  • "Write a note to file explaining what really happened in March." A note written now, for the dispute, is a reconstruction, and it may be disclosable.
  • "Just keep this between us." There is no informal circle in a dispute, except the one your lawyer defines.
  • Anything to the contractor in anger, by email, message or phone.

Say that out loud now.

Nobody deletes, edits or rewrites anything. A bad email that is preserved can be explained. A deleted one cannot.

The question behind the question

  • "Should we clean up the drive?" really asks: will I be blamed for what is in it? Answer the fear: "The record protects you more than it hurts you. Keep it intact and let counsel deal with what it shows."
  • "Can I write up my side while it is fresh?" asks: will anyone believe me? Answer: "Yes, but only at counsel's request and addressed to counsel, so it is prepared for advice."
  • "Do we keep talking to their site team?" asks: does the job stop? Answer: "The job continues. Talk about the work, record the work, and leave the claim to the claims process."

When to stay silent

When the project manager defends his March emails at length, do not argue the merits in the room. Let him finish, then say: "Thank you. Tell counsel that." When someone asks you to predict the outcome, say nothing beyond "We will value it properly." And when the contractor's director rings you that afternoon, listen, acknowledge, and say you will respond in writing. Silence costs nothing; an unguarded concession on the phone can be quoted for two years.

Holding your state

You will be angry. A claim for 2,400,000 dollars on a job you believe the contractor ran badly feels like an accusation. Notice the anger, name it to yourself, and decide that no decision is taken while it is the loudest thing in the room. Kema's practice from Week 4 applies: a few slow breaths, seated, before you speak. Then work the list. The developer who stays procedural in the first hour looks, to a tribunal reading the record later, like the reasonable party, and very often that is what wins the close calls.

A worked sequence

Hypothetical, the next 48 hours. By noon: acknowledgement sent to the contractor, one paragraph, reserving rights. By 3 in the afternoon: counsel's written hold issued to six named custodians, auto-deletion suspended on the project messaging group, document controller exports the shared drive's version history. By the next morning: all six confirm the hold in writing; the site manager's phone is imaged by a forensic provider; the claims register is updated with the contractual response period and counsel's limitation view; the lender is informed in a short factual note. Cost: a forensic imaging fee and a few hours of counsel's time. Value: a record that cannot be attacked.

Decision journals: a monthly thread

This month's thread is the decision journal, which Kema introduced in Week 2: a short dated note, written when you make a significant decision, recording what you decided, what you knew, what you expected to happen and how confident you were. It is the owner's personal contemporaneous record, and it does two jobs. It makes you a better decision-maker, because you can later compare what you expected with what happened, and it is evidence of what you knew and when.

Two cautions. A decision journal may be disclosable in a dispute, so write it as you would want a tribunal to read it: facts and reasoning, not insults or speculation about others. And never edit an old entry; add a dated new one. Ask counsel how to keep it alongside the project record.

What to tell the lender, and when

Many loan agreements require the borrower to report material claims or litigation promptly, and some treat an unreported one as a default; verify that against your own loan documents. The note should be short and factual: a claim has been received, its amount and basis as stated by the contractor, that the job continues, that counsel is reviewing it, and when you will send a fuller assessment. Do not argue the merits to the lender, and do not forecast the outcome. A lender who hears about a claim from you, early and calmly, extends trust; one who hears about it from a lien search does not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a well-meant instruction in the first hour, to tidy, rewrite or keep things quiet, that later reads as an attempt to destroy or shape evidence. The control is a fixed first-hour script: freeze everything, call counsel, issue a written hold, acknowledge formally, and keep the work and the claim on separate tracks.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner fires back a detailed rebuttal the same day. It commits him to positions before the record is reviewed, may contain admissions, and sets the tone for the whole dispute. Acknowledge now; respond properly within the contract's period, after review.

Callback

On Day 2 of Week 81, a developer lost a strong claim because talks ran past the deadlines. The first-hour meeting is where the calendar starts: put the contractual response period and counsel's limitation view in the claims register the same day.

Recap

When a claim arrives, freeze the record, call counsel, issue a written hold to named custodians including phones, acknowledge formally and respond later. Never tidy, rewrite or reply in anger. Hear the fear behind the team's questions. Stay silent on the merits. Keep a decision journal you would be content to see read aloud. Professional sign-off required: dispute counsel.

Next: Kema's Week 82 review: six questions, a Red Pen site diary and the two-minute boardroom drill.
checklist: The moment a claim arrives, I instruct that nothing is deleted, edited, moved or renamed.
Counsel issues a written hold to named custodians the same day.
Every custodian confirms the hold in writing.
Phones and messaging apps used for project work are preserved.
I acknowledge the claim formally and respond within the contract period after review.
I never ask anyone to write a note to file except at counsel's request.
I keep the work and the claim on separate tracks.
I update the claims register with response and limitation dates that day.
head: Field checklist
speak: The first two hours after a claim arrives decide whether your record is evidence or a liability. In the room, say it plainly: nobody deletes, edits, moves or renames anything, on the drive, in email or on phones. Counsel issues a written hold today and everyone confirms it. If someone sent an email they regret, they tell counsel, because a bad email that is preserved can be explained and a deleted one cannot. Acknowledge the claim in one paragraph and respond properly within the contract's period. Never say tidy up the files, never ask for a note to file, never reply in anger. Hear the fear behind the team's questions and answer that. Stay silent on the merits. Hold your state: notice the anger and decide nothing while it is the loudest thing in the room. Then keep the job and the claim on separate tracks.
terms: Custodian — a person who holds documents or data relevant to a dispute and must preserve them under a hold.
Note to file — a memorandum written to record events; if written after a dispute begins, it is a reconstruction and may be disclosable.
Forensic imaging — an exact, verifiable copy of a device's data taken by a specialist so its contents can be preserved and later examined.

hostile.q: Your project manager's March emails admit the drawings were late. Did anyone on your side delete anything after our claim arrived?
hostile.a: No. A written hold went to six named custodians on the day your claim arrived, each confirmed it, auto-deletion was suspended and the site manager's phone was forensically imaged. The March emails have been produced in full, including the ones you are quoting. They say drawings were late on two packages; our response deals with why those two packages did not delay completion.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 82 Review: Control, Evidence, Privilege and the First Hour
summary: Six questions on document control, contemporaneous records, the dollar value of records, privilege and preservation, reverse engineering a delay award and the first hour after a claim. Then a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical daily site report with planted defects, and the two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: the record made at the time, controlled, preserved and checked against reality, is the only version of the project that a lender, a tribunal or a buyer will believe.

Recall

Q. What is a seat of arbitration, and why does it matter?

A. The legal home of the arbitration, which decides which country's courts supervise it and hear any challenge to the award. It is a separate choice from the governing law.

Q. What is a risk trigger?

A. An agreed, observable event or measurement that tells the risk owner a risk is starting to happen and the planned response should begin.

Q. What was the root cause in the Week 75 post-mortem on governance capture?

A. That the same people controlled both sides of transactions with no independent check, so related-party dealing went unchallenged until it was too late.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, records are the least glamorous subject in this course and among the most valuable. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the four parts of document control?

Answer: A register of controlled documents with current revisions; revision control, with superseded versions marked and withdrawn; transmittals proving what was issued to whom and when; and one controlled home that is the source of truth.

Question 2. Why does a contemporaneous record outweigh a witness?

Answer: Because it was made at the time, in the normal course of work, by someone with knowledge, before anyone had a reason to shade it. Memory fades and is coloured by the dispute.

Question 3. What was Rule 82, from Grenfell?

Answer: Never accept a test report, certificate or product claim as evidence until you have read what was actually tested, in what configuration, and confirmed it matches what is being installed; then keep that comparison in the record.

Question 4. How can 180,000 dollars of undocumented rent cost 3,000,000 dollars?

Answer: A buyer excludes income it cannot verify, and value is NOI divided by the cap rate. At 6 percent, 180,000 dollars of NOI supports 3,000,000 dollars of price.

Question 5. What do privilege and preservation each require?

Answer: Privilege protects confidential lawyer-client advice and some litigation communications, not business documents, and is lost by sharing outside the circle. Preservation requires keeping everything relevant once a dispute is reasonably anticipated, under a written hold covering phones and messages.

Question 6. In the first hour after a claim arrives, what are the five actions?

Answer: Freeze the record, call counsel, issue a written hold to named custodians with confirmations, acknowledge the claim formally without arguing it, and update the claims register and inform the lender.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Vera built document control and the contemporaneous record. Ford and Cole took Grenfell Tower as a failure of records that described a different building, giving Rule 82. Nadia priced records through draw delay, audit cost and exit value. Vera taught privilege, preservation, spoliation and retention. Petra reverse engineered a delay award and found 20 days lost to three missing records. Vera ran the first hour after a claim.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical owner's inspector's daily report and find the defects before reading on.

Daily Report. Project: Riverside Apartments. Date: Tuesday. Weather: fine. Contractor on site: good numbers. Work: frame level 4 progressing, some delay on steel. Instructions: told the site manager the balcony detail changes, per architect. Visitors: engineer. Issues: as discussed. Photos: on my phone. Signed: J.

The defects. First, the date has a weekday but no calendar date, so the report cannot be tied to a schedule or a claim. Second, "fine" weather gives no rain, wind or temperature, which matter for weather delay and concrete. Third, "good numbers" records no headcount by trade, which is exactly the evidence that lost block 1 of the Day 5 award. Fourth, "some delay on steel" gives no cause, quantity or expected date and does not say whether steel was late to site or late to erect. Fifth, the balcony instruction was oral, with no drawing reference, revision or confirmation, which is an unrecorded change in the making. Sixth, "engineer" names no person or firm, and "as discussed" records nothing. Seventh, photographs held on a personal phone are outside the project record and may be lost. Eighth, "J." is not an identifiable author, and there is no time of writing.

The rewrite in outline: full date and time written; rain, wind and temperature; headcount by trade checked against the contractor's return; a specific note on the steel, citing the delivery register; the balcony instruction confirmed in writing that day with drawing number and revision; the visitor's name and firm; each issue stated as a fact; photographs uploaded to the project record with location; full name and role.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "Why are you spending money on a document controller?" Record it, then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because every number you rely on rests on a record. The lender funds draws on documents; a missing lien waiver delays cash every month. A buyer pays only for income it can verify; on a building like ours, a handful of unsigned leases can move the price by millions at our cap rate. In a dispute, the tribunal believes records made at the time over anyone's memory, and on a typical delay claim a few missing logs can cost hundreds of thousands. So we run one controlled document home, issue every drawing with a transmittal, require daily reports, keep our own inspector's diary, delivery register and submittal log, and check safety-critical products against their real test reports. If a claim arrives, we freeze everything under a written hold the same day. The cost is a small fraction of one percent of the budget, and it protects value at every stage."

Score yourself. Did you lead with the bottom line? Did you give a dollar example? Did you mention preservation? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

Kema's field exercise

Before next week, run a ten-minute test on any project you can see, your own or one you are studying. Pick one day, three months ago. Try to answer four questions from the record alone, without asking anyone: how many workers were on site by trade; which drawing revision was in use for the main work that day; what instructions were given, and to whom; and what the weather was. Time yourself. If you cannot answer all four in ten minutes, you have found the gap that a tribunal, a lender or a buyer would find. Write down which record was missing and what it would take to keep it, then add that to your project's document control plan.

This is also a drill for your own habits. Most people discover that their own notes are thinner than they believed. Better to find that out on a quiet afternoon than in a hearing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a record that exists in fragments, in inboxes, phones and memories, so it cannot be found, trusted or preserved when it is needed. The control is one home, a register, transmittals, contractual daily reports, owner's own logs and a hold procedure ready before any claim.

The beginner's mistake

Treating records as the contractor's job. The contractor keeps records for its claims. The owner must keep its own, and check the contractor's against them, every week.

Callback

In Week 72, REGA and Cole taught that integrity is a control system, not a personality trait. Records are that control system made visible: a team that writes things down at the time, keeps them and never edits them later is a team whose word will be believed.

Recap

Control the documents, keep contemporaneous records, check paper against reality, price the gaps, protect privileged advice, preserve everything once a dispute is foreseeable, and run the first hour from a script. Rule 82 keeps the record honest about the building.

head: The six questions
speak: Here is the week in a minute. The record made at the time is the only version of the project anyone will believe. Run document control: a register, revision control, transmittals and one home. Require contemporaneous records, daily reports, photographs and minutes, and keep your own inspector's diary, delivery register and submittal log. Check every safety-critical product against its real test report, which is Rule 82, from Grenfell. Records are money: a missing lien waiver slows draws, and unverified rent is excluded from price at the cap rate. Privilege protects legal advice, not business documents, and sharing advice can lose it. Once a dispute is foreseeable, preserve everything under a written hold, including phones, because destroying evidence can lose the case. And when a claim arrives, freeze the record, call counsel, acknowledge formally, and never tidy, rewrite or reply in anger.
terms: Adverse inference — a tribunal's assumption that missing evidence would have hurt the party responsible for losing it.
Retention schedule — a written list of record categories with how long each is kept and how it is destroyed when the period ends.
Estoppel certificate — a tenant's signed statement confirming lease terms and rent, often requested in due diligence.

hostile.q: Your inspector's diary is in a spreadsheet. How do I know it was not written after the dispute started?
hostile.a: Because it lives in our controlled project drive, which keeps a version history with timestamps for every entry, and each week's entries were attached to an email to your site manager the following Monday, which your own records will show. We will produce the native file with its version history, and your expert is welcome to examine it.
